title: MATH GAOKAO - 346
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the defining property of a simple random sample.
questions.question: Which sampling method gives every individual in the population an equal chance of being selected and every sample of a given size an equal chance of being chosen?
questions.explanation: A simple random sample is selected so that every individual has the same chance of being chosen and every possible sample of the required size has the same chance of being selected. Convenience sampling selects easily available individuals and does not guarantee equal chance.
questions.hint: Recall the sampling method based on equal probability for every individual and every possible sample.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize stratified sampling as sampling within each subgroup of a population.
questions.question: Which sampling method divides the population into groups called strata and then takes a random sample from each stratum?
questions.explanation: In stratified random sampling, the population is first divided into strata based on some characteristic, and then a random sample is drawn from each stratum. Cluster sampling instead selects whole groups or clusters.
questions.hint: Focus on whether samples are taken from every subgroup or from selected groups.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish cluster sampling from stratified sampling.
questions.question: Which sampling method divides the population into clusters and then randomly selects entire clusters for study?
questions.explanation: Cluster sampling divides the population into clusters, randomly selects some clusters, and then studies all or part of the selected clusters. Stratified sampling instead samples from every stratum.
questions.hint: Consider whether whole groups are selected or samples are taken from every subgroup.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the sampling interval for systematic sampling.
questions.question: A population of \(100\) individuals is sampled systematically to obtain \(10\) individuals. What is the sampling interval \(k\)?
questions.explanation:
For systematic sampling, the interval is
\[
k=\frac{\text{population size}}{\text{sample size}}.
\]
Thus,
\[
k=\frac{100}{10}=10.
\]
Therefore, the sampling interval is \(10\).
questions.hint: Divide the population size by the desired sample size.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a convenience sample from a described sampling procedure.
questions.question: A researcher surveys only people leaving a fitness center about their exercise habits. This sample is best described as:
questions.explanation: The researcher chooses people who are easily available at the fitness center. This is convenience sampling because the sample is selected based on ease of access, not random selection from the whole population.
questions.hint: Consider whether the sample is chosen randomly or because the individuals are easy to reach.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a voluntary response sample and its possible bias.
questions.question: A television program asks viewers to call in and vote on a topic. The resulting sample is best described as:
questions.explanation: The viewers decide whether to participate by calling in. This is a voluntary response sample. Such samples often overrepresent people with strong opinions and are generally biased.
questions.hint: Ask whether the individuals themselves choose to participate in the sample.

questions.learningObjective: Choose the correct procedure for obtaining a simple random sample.
questions.question: Which procedure correctly selects a simple random sample of \(20\) students from a school?

options.label: A
options.text: Number all students and use a random number generator to select \(20\) distinct numbers.

options.label: B
options.text: Select the first \(20\) students who enter the school.

questions.explanation: A simple random sample requires a random mechanism that gives every student the same chance of selection. Numbering all students and using a random number generator to select \(20\) distinct numbers accomplishes this. Selecting the first \(20\) students who enter is a convenience sample, not a simple random sample.
questions.hint: Look for the procedure that uses a genuine random selection from the whole population.

questions.learningObjective: Allocate a stratified sample proportionally to strata sizes.
questions.question: A school has \(300\) boys and \(200\) girls. A proportional stratified sample of \(50\) students is to be selected. How many boys and girls should be selected?
questions.explanation:
The total population is
\[
300+200=500.
\]
The proportion of boys is
\[
\frac{300}{500}=0.6,
\]
so the number of boys in the sample is
\[
0.6(50)=30.
\]
The proportion of girls is
\[
\frac{200}{500}=0.4,
\]
so the number of girls is
\[
0.4(50)=20.
\]
Therefore, the sample should contain \(30\) boys and \(20\) girls.
questions.hint: Use each subgroup proportion multiplied by the total sample size.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an appropriate sampling frame for a school survey.
questions.question: A researcher wants to sample students from a school. Which is the most appropriate sampling frame?

options.label: A
options.text: A list of students in one class

options.label: B
options.text: A complete list of all enrolled students

questions.explanation: A sampling frame is the list from which the sample is drawn. To represent the whole school, the frame should include all enrolled students. A list of students in only one class would exclude most of the population and could produce a biased sample.
questions.hint: Consider which list contains the entire target population.

questions.learningObjective: Choose a sampling method that is least likely to produce bias.
questions.question: Which method is least likely to produce a biased sample?

options.label: A
options.text: Randomly selecting individuals from a complete list of the population

options.label: B
options.text: Asking for volunteers at a shopping mall

questions.explanation: Random selection from a complete list of the population gives all individuals a known and equal chance of being selected, which reduces bias. Asking for volunteers at a shopping mall tends to overrepresent people who are present at that location and willing to participate, so it is more likely to be biased.
questions.hint: Compare whether the method uses random selection from the full population or depends on who happens to volunteer.
